posts.topic: How to check your boiler pressure and top it up safely
posts.facebook:
📉 Boiler pressure dropped below 1 bar? Here's how to top it up yourself:

1️⃣ Find the filling loop — usually a silver braided hose under the boiler
2️⃣ Open the valves slowly until the gauge reads 1.5 bar
3️⃣ Close the valves and restart the boiler

If it drops again within a few weeks, that's a sign of a leak or internal fault — worth getting checked before it becomes a bigger problem.

https://bettercallwes.co.uk/services/boiler-repair.html

posts.topic: Cold radiators — how to bleed them yourself
posts.facebook:
🌡️ Got a radiator that's hot at the bottom but cold at the top? It needs bleeding.

Here's how:

1️⃣ Turn the heating off and let the radiator cool
2️⃣ Use a radiator key (or flat-head screwdriver) on the bleed valve — usually top right
3️⃣ Turn slowly anticlockwise until you hear hissing air
4️⃣ When water starts to drip, close the valve
5️⃣ Check your boiler pressure afterwards — top up if needed

posts.topic: How to bleed a radiator
posts.facebook:
🔧 Cold spots on your radiators? Bleed them.

How to do it:
1. Turn heating on and wait 20 mins
2. Feel each radiator — cold at the top = trapped air
3. Turn heating OFF and let it cool
4. Use a radiator key to open the bleed valve (anti-clockwise)
5. Air hisses out → water appears → close the valve
6. Check boiler pressure and top up if needed

If they're still cold after bleeding, it could be sludge — power flushing fixes that.

posts.topic: How to top up boiler pressure safely
posts.facebook:
📊 Boiler pressure too low? Here's how to top it up safely.

Your boiler pressure should sit between 1–1.5 bar when cold.

1. Turn the boiler OFF and let it cool
2. Find the filling loop — usually a silver/grey braided hose under the boiler
3. Open both valves (quarter turn) until pressure reaches 1.2–1.5 bar
4. Close both valves — make sure they're fully closed
5. Turn the boiler back on

⚠️ If pressure rises above 2.5 bar, don't use the boiler — call an engineer.
⚠️ If it keeps dropping, there's a leak — call me.

posts.topic: Frozen condensate pipe — how to fix it yourself
posts.facebook:
🥶 Boiler stopped working in cold weather? Check the condensate pipe.

Modern condensate boilers have a plastic pipe (usually white or grey) that exits outside the property. In freezing temperatures it can ice up and cause the boiler to lock out.

How to fix it yourself:
1. Find the pipe outside (usually near the boiler on an external wall)
2. Pour warm water (NOT boiling) along the frozen section
3. Reset the boiler once it thaws

If this keeps happening, the pipe may need insulating or rerouting.

🔥 Ignition fault / F28 / E133 — gas supply or pilot issue
🌡️ Overheat — pump, sensor or flow problem

One reset is fine. If it locks out again, stop resetting and get it diagnosed — you could make a small fault into a big one.

posts.topic: How to spot a gas leak at home
posts.facebook:
⚠️ Suspect a gas leak? Know the signs — they can save lives:

👃 Rotten egg smell (added to gas on purpose)
💨 Hissing near a pipe, meter or appliance
🌱 Dead patch of grass near your gas supply outside
🤕 Headaches, dizziness or drowsiness that eases when you leave the house

If you suspect a leak: open windows, don't switch anything electrical on or off, get out, and call the National Gas Emergency line on 0800 111 999.

posts.facebook:
💧 Tap dripping? It's almost always one of three things:

1. Worn washer (traditional taps) — cheap to replace, 10 min job
2. Faulty ceramic cartridge (modern mixer/monobloc taps) — cartridge swap
3. Worn O-ring at the spout base — new seal

A single drip doesn't sound like much, but it can waste over 20 litres a day and eat into your water bill. Usually a quick fix before it turns into a steady leak.

📊 Your boiler's pressure gauge — what should it actually say?

✅ 1 to 1.5 bar when the system is cold
🔥 Up to around 2 bar while the heating is running
⚠️ Below 1 bar — heating struggles, boiler may lock out
🚨 Above 2.5 bar — too high, often an overfilled system or a tired expansion vessel

Topping up now and then is normal. Topping up every week isn't — that's a leak or a part on its way out, and it's worth catching before winter.

posts.topic: Why one radiator is always cold — balancing basics
posts.facebook:
🥶 One radiator roasting, another barely warm? That's not a broken rad — it's an unbalanced system.

Hot water is lazy. It takes the easiest route back to the boiler, so the radiators nearest it hog the flow and the far ones get leftovers.

Balancing fixes it: the lockshield valve (the capped one) gets closed down slightly on the greedy rads, pushing flow out to the lazy ones.

⚠️ If a rad is cold at the BOTTOM though, that's sludge, not balance — different problem, different fix.

Save this for the first cold week of autumn.

posts.topic: TRV numbers explained — they're temperatures, not power
posts.facebook:
🌡️ Those numbers on your radiator valves aren't volume knobs. They're target temperatures:

❄️ * (frost) ≈ 7°C — pipes protected, room cold
2️⃣ ≈ 17°C — perfect for bedrooms (you sleep better cooler)
3️⃣ ≈ 20°C — the living-room sweet spot
5️⃣ ≈ 25°C+ — a greenhouse

The valve isn't 'pushing harder' on 5 — it just keeps heating until the room hits a higher temperature, then stops.

💡 So cranking every rad to 5 doesn't heat the house faster. It just heats it longer, and you pay for the difference.

Save this — your spare room is on the wrong number right now.

The numbers on thermostatic radiator valves are widely misunderstood — they're target room temperatures, not power levels. As a rough guide, the frost symbol holds about 7°C to protect pipework, setting 2 gives around 17°C (ideal for bedrooms, where most people sleep better cooler), setting 3 is roughly 20°C for living spaces, and 5 is well over 25°C. A valve on 5 isn't pushing heat harder; it simply keeps the radiator on until the room reaches a higher temperature. That's why turning every radiator to maximum doesn't warm the house faster — it just runs the heating longer, at your expense. Set each room to its job and the savings follow. posts.topic: What your gas hob's flame colour is telling you
posts.facebook:
🔵 Quick kitchen safety check you can do tonight: look at your hob's flame.

✅ Crisp blue with a steady cone = clean, complete combustion. All good.
⚠️ Lazy yellow or orange tips, flames that lift and flutter, or soot on your pan bottoms = incomplete combustion. That means the burner needs attention — and incomplete combustion is what produces carbon monoxide.

A yellow flame isn't a 'keep an eye on it'. Stop using that burner and get it checked.

(And if you ever smell gas: 0800 111 999, free, 24/7 — before anything else.)

posts.topic: How to balance your radiators
posts.facebook:
♨️ One room roasting, another one never warm? Your radiators probably need balancing — not replacing.

Here's what's happening. Hot water is lazy. It takes the easiest route, so the rads nearest the boiler hog it and the far ones get the leftovers.

Balancing just slows the greedy ones down so everything gets a fair share:

🔧 Open every lockshield valve fully, run the heating, note which rads warm first
🔧 Close the lockshield on the fastest rad almost shut, then open it about a quarter turn
🔧 Work outwards, giving the furthest rads the most flow
🔧 Give it an hour and check again

It costs nothing but an afternoon, and it's the single most overlooked fix in British heating.

Save this for when you need it.

posts.topic: What the numbers on your TRV actually mean
posts.facebook:
🌡️ The numbers on your radiator valve are not a speed dial. Nearly everyone gets this wrong.

Cranking a TRV to 5 does not heat the room faster. It heats it to a higher temperature — and then it sits there, roasting, until you notice and open a window. Which is heating the street.

Roughly what the numbers mean:

❄️ ✱ — frost protection only
1️⃣ around 10°C
2️⃣ around 15°C
3️⃣ around 20°C — where most living rooms want to be
4️⃣ around 25°C
5️⃣ around 30°C — you will never want this

Set it to 3, leave it alone, and let it do its job. And don't put a TRV in the room with your thermostat — the two will argue and the thermostat always wins.

Save this for when you need it.

posts.topic: Frozen condensate pipe — the fix you can do yourself
posts.facebook:
🧊 Boiler dead the morning after a hard frost? Before you ring anyone — check the condensate pipe.

It's the white plastic pipe running out through the wall to a drain. In a cold snap the water inside it freezes, the boiler can't push its condensate out, so it locks itself off and throws a fault code. Nothing is broken. It's the boiler protecting itself.

The fix, if you can reach it safely:

🫖 Warm water along the outside of the pipe — a kettle that's boiled and stood for ten minutes, never boiling water straight from the spout
♨️ Or a hot water bottle held against the elbow, which is where it usually freezes
🔄 Then reset the boiler

If it keeps happening, the pipe wants lagging or rerouting properly — that bit's me.

Save this for when you need it.

It's the white plastic pipe running through the wall to a drain, and in freezing weather the water inside it turns to ice. If you can reach the pipe safely, pour warm water along the outside of it, using a kettle that has boiled and stood for ten minutes rather than water straight off the boil, or hold a hot water bottle against the elbow where ice usually forms. posts.topic: Why your pipes bang and creak at night
posts.facebook:
🌙 Pipes banging and ticking after you've gone to bed? It's almost never haunted. It's usually one of four things.

🔨 Water hammer — a bang when a tap or the washing machine shuts off. The water was moving, then suddenly wasn't, and the shock has nowhere to go. A properly-fitted arrestor kills it.
🎵 Ticking as the heating goes off — copper expanding and contracting, rubbing against a floor joist or a clip that's too tight. Annoying, harmless, fixable.
🌊 Gurgling — air in the system. Bleed the rads.
🫧 A constant hiss or trickle when nothing's running — that one's not harmless. Something is passing water somewhere. Get it looked at.

Three of those you can live with. The fourth one is a bill quietly getting bigger.

Save this for when you need it.

posts.topic: How I decide the order of the day
posts.facebook:
🗺️ People assume the diary runs first come, first served. It doesn't, and I've never pretended otherwise.

It runs on who's actually cold.

The order, roughly:

1️⃣ No heat or no hot water, and someone vulnerable in the house — young kids, elderly, unwell. That's the top and it isn't close
2️⃣ No heat or no hot water at all
3️⃣ Anything getting worse while it waits — an active leak, a system losing pressure
4️⃣ Everything else, in sensible geographic order so I'm not crossing the city four times

Which means occasionally I'll ring and ask to move you. If I do, it's because someone's in a worse spot than you — and if it's ever you in that spot, I'd want the same done for you.

posts.topic: Real job — the toilet that never stopped filling
posts.facebook:
🚽 "It's only a bit of a trickle, it's been like that for ages."

That trickle was costing more than the repair. Every single month.

A cistern that never quite stops filling is water going straight from your meter into the sewer, twenty-four hours a day, for however long you've ignored it. Cistern lid off, new mechanism in, done inside the hour.

If yours has a permanent ripple in the pan — that's it. That's the sign.

posts.topic: Covering Romsey
posts.facebook:
📍 Romsey — lovely town, brutal water.

If you live out that way you already know. The kettle furs up in a fortnight. There's a permanent white ring in the loo. That's not your imagination, and it's not just an annoyance — it's the single biggest thing shortening the life of your heating.

Scale plates out inside heat exchangers, chokes flow, and makes your boiler work harder to shift less heat. It's why boilers in hard water areas kettle years earlier than the same model somewhere soft.

What actually helps: an annual service so it's caught early, and a scale reducer on the mains if you haven't got one. Neither is exciting. Both add years.

Romsey, North Baddesley, Nursling, Chilworth — all covered.

Comment SERVICE and I'll DM you my service-booking link.

Every failed part is a story about how something dies. Hold thirty burnt connectors from the same model and you stop guessing — you start recognising. You walk into a house, hear the symptom, and you already know what you're going to find because you've got the evidence in a box at home.

There's a second reason. I'll happily hand you the old part when I've finished. It's yours. You paid for its replacement — you're entitled to see what you paid for.

Half the mistrust in this trade would vanish if more people did that.

posts.facebook:

1️⃣ Electrics off at the consumer unit for that part of the house. Water and ceiling roses are a genuinely dangerous combination. This one is first for a reason

5️⃣ Then ring someone

posts.topic: What the colour of your hob flame tells you
posts.facebook:
🔵 Go and look at your hob. The flame should be crisp and blue. Nothing else.

What the colours mean:

🔵 Blue, steady, sharp — burning properly. Nothing to do
🟠 Orange or yellow, lazy and floppy — incomplete combustion. That means it's not getting the air it needs, and incomplete combustion is how carbon monoxide gets made
⚫ Sooty black marks around the burner or on the pan bottoms — same story, happening for a while now
💨 A flame that lifts off the burner or roars — also wrong

One caveat: some hobs have a deliberate yellow tip, and gas fires with fake coals are meant to look yellow. Those are by design.

But a hob burning orange isn't a quirk. It's a message. Get it looked at properly.

Save this for when you need it.

posts.topic: Five checks before the heating season starts
posts.facebook:
🔧 Five things worth checking now, before the heating goes on properly.

1️⃣ Pressure. Cold system should sit around 1 to 1.5 bar. If it's dropped over the summer, something's letting go somewhere.

2️⃣ Fire it up for twenty minutes. A fault that's been sat dormant since March will show itself now, not in the first frost.

3️⃣ Walk round the rads. Cold at the top means air. Cold at the bottom means sludge — different problem, different fix.

4️⃣ Check the condensate pipe outside. If it's exposed and unlagged, it will freeze and shut the boiler down.

5️⃣ Test the thermostat and the timer. Batteries die quietly.

Ten minutes of this in August saves a very cold, very expensive week later on.

Save this for when you need it.

posts.facebook:

That combination narrows things down fast. If the boiler will heat water on demand but won't send anything to the rads, the burner and the pump are usually fine — it's the bit that decides where the hot water goes.

Multimeter on the actuator confirmed it was getting the signal and doing nothing about it. Cartridge and actuator swapped, system rebalanced, every rad checked warm before I packed up.

Early on in my career. Customer said the boiler was losing pressure. I found a weeping valve, changed it, topped the system up, wrote it up as done and drove off feeling pretty good about myself.

Four days later, same call. Same pressure drop.

The first fault I found wasn't wrong. It just wasn't the whole story — and I'd stopped looking the moment I found something that fitted.

Now I don't close a job on the first thing I find. I check the system holds after the fix, not just that the fix looked right.

Costs me twenty minutes. Has saved customers thousands.

posts.facebook:
♨️ Bleed your radiators now, not in the first cold week.

Air collects in a heating system all summer while it's sat doing nothing. Come the first proper burn, that air is sat at the top of your rads stopping them heating and making the boiler work harder for less.

How to do it properly:

1️⃣ Heating off, system cool
2️⃣ Start with the radiator furthest from the boiler
3️⃣ Bleed key into the square socket at the top corner, quarter turn, cloth underneath
4️⃣ Let the hiss run until water comes, then close it
5️⃣ Work back towards the boiler, upstairs last
6️⃣ Check the pressure afterwards — bleeding drops it

That last step is the one everybody forgets, then wonders why the boiler locks out the next morning.

Not because it's a bad tool. Because of how people use it.

posts.topic: Check your boiler pressure after a summer off
posts.facebook:
📉 Go and look at your boiler's pressure gauge. I'll wait.

A cold system should read somewhere between 1 and 1.5 bar. Most boilers lock themselves out below about 0.5.

Here's why now matters. Over the summer your heating has barely run, so a slow loss of pressure produces no symptoms at all — no cold rads, no noise, nothing. The needle just creeps down quietly for months.

Then the heating goes on properly, the boiler asks the system for everything it's got, and it locks out on low pressure in the first cold week of the year.

If yours has dropped since spring, that's not normal. Water has gone somewhere. Topping it up gets you going, but it doesn't answer the question of where.

Two minutes today. Genuinely worth it.

posts.topic: Real job — what came out of the magnetic filter
posts.facebook:
🪣 Real job: this is what came out of one magnetic filter.

Jet black. Like pouring old engine oil into a bucket. And that's the stuff the filter caught — which means it's the stuff that wasn't circulating through the pump, the heat exchanger and every radiator in the house.

That black sludge is iron oxide. It forms wherever water, steel and oxygen live together, which is every heating system ever built. Left alone it settles in the bottom of radiators, eats pump bearings and blocks the narrow waterways in a heat exchanger.

Symptoms to watch for: cold at the bottom of a radiator, a boiler that kettles, rooms that take forever to warm through.

If you've got a filter, it should be emptied at every service. If you haven't got one, that's the single best upgrade you can make to an older system.

posts.topic: Lag the condensate pipe before the first freeze
posts.facebook:
🧊 The single most common reason a boiler dies in a cold snap isn't the boiler. It's a plastic pipe.

Your condensate pipe carries acidic water away from the boiler. If part of it runs outside and it isn't insulated, a hard frost turns that water to ice, the pipe blocks, the boiler detects it and shuts itself down to protect you.

Hundreds of Southampton homes lose their heating this way on the same night, every single winter.

The fix, if it happens: pour warm — not boiling — water along the outside pipe, then reset the boiler.

The prevention, which is better: go outside now and look. A white or grey plastic pipe coming out of the wall near the boiler. If it's bare, lag it. Foam insulation is a few quid from any merchant and takes ten minutes.

Doing it in August beats doing it in the dark at minus two.

posts.topic: How to spot a tired central heating pump
posts.facebook:
🔊 Your central heating pump is the component nobody thinks about until it stops. Here's how to catch it on the way out.

1️⃣ A humming or buzzing that's noticeably louder than last year — bearings wearing.
2️⃣ Radiators furthest from the boiler taking much longer to warm than they used to, with no other change.
3️⃣ The pump body running hot to the touch while the pipes either side are barely warm — it's spinning but not moving water.
4️⃣ Heating that works fine on a mild day and can't cope on a cold one.

Pumps very rarely fail overnight. They fade, and because they fade slowly, people adjust to it — turning the thermostat up, leaving the heating on longer, paying more every month without realising why.

Best time to find a tired pump is before the system is asked to work hard.

Comment SERVICE and I'll DM you my service-booking link.

posts.topic: Why autumn is the cheapest time to fix a boiler
posts.facebook:
📅 Same fault. Same boiler. Same engineer. Different price. Here's why.

In the cold months a repair costs more, and it isn't a stitch-up — it's supply and demand doing what it always does.

🔧 Parts. Merchants run down on the common failures because every engineer in the city is buying the same fan and the same PCB in the same fortnight. Sold out means sourcing further afield, which costs more and takes longer.

🔧 Time. A fault that's diagnosed calmly and fixed in one visit is cheaper than one where you're heating the house with electric heaters while parts are chased.

🔧 Scale. A weeping seal found now is a seal. Found in January, after it's been dripping onto a circuit board for three months, it's a seal and a board.

Nothing about my rates changes with the weather. The size of the job does.

posts.topic: The hardest thing about being self-employed
posts.facebook:
💭 People assume the hardest part of working for yourself is the money. It isn't.

It's that there's nobody to ask.

When you're employed and you hit something you've never seen before, you turn round and there's a bloke who's seen it twice. When you're on your own, you're stood in a stranger's kitchen with their heating in bits and everybody in the room thinks you already know the answer.

You learn to be comfortable saying 'give me a minute'. You build a group chat of people you trust. You read manuals in the van at half seven at night.

But the moment itself — that quiet moment where it's just you and a problem — that never fully stops being uncomfortable.

I think that's healthy, honestly. The day it stops feeling like that is probably the day I start cutting corners.

posts.topic: Test your CO alarm before the heating goes on
posts.facebook:
⚠️ Carbon monoxide has no smell, no colour and no taste. Your only warning is an alarm — and only if it's working.

Two minutes, right now:

🔘 Press the test button. It should be loud enough to be unpleasant.
🔘 Check the date on the back. Sensors expire, usually after seven to ten years. An expired alarm that still beeps is not protecting you.
🔘 Check where it is. Roughly head height, 1 to 3 metres from the appliance, not right next to it and not in a cupboard.

Symptoms to know: headaches, dizziness, nausea, feeling better when you leave the house. If you suspect CO — get everyone out, open doors and windows, and ring the National Gas Emergency Service on 0800 111 999.

Heating season is when boilers work hardest, which is exactly when a poorly burning appliance shows itself.

posts.topic: Why I don't chase big contracts
posts.facebook:
🚫 I get approached fairly regularly about contract work. Blocks of flats, letting agency portfolios, that sort of thing. Steady volume, guaranteed invoices.

I say no, nearly every time.

Not because it's bad work. Because of what it does to the work I already do.

Contract volume means targets. Targets mean minutes per property. Minutes per property means the bit where I sit down and explain what's actually wrong gets cut first, because it's the only part nobody's measuring.

That conversation is the job, as far as I'm concerned. It's the difference between someone understanding their heating and someone just paying to make a problem go away.

I'd rather do fewer jobs properly than more jobs quickly and slowly become someone I wouldn't hire.

It's not the fastest way to grow. It's the only version of this I actually want.

posts.topic: What to do before you turn the heating on for the first time
posts.facebook:
🎚️ Don't just flick the heating on and hope. Do this first — it takes about half an hour and it saves the classic first-cold-week panic.

1️⃣ Set the thermostat well above room temperature so the system definitely fires.
2️⃣ Run it for at least twenty minutes, not two. Faults show up under load, not at start-up.
3️⃣ Walk every room and put a hand on every radiator, top and bottom.
4️⃣ Open all the TRVs fully while you do it, so nothing is being throttled and wrongly blamed.
5️⃣ Listen. Kettling, ticking, gurgling — note which room and when.
6️⃣ Check the pressure again once it's hot. It rises when warm, which is normal, but it shouldn't be near the red.

Anything odd, you've found it in August with the diary open, rather than in a cold week with everyone else calling.

Save this for when you need it.

posts.topic: Lag your exposed pipes before the cold arrives
posts.facebook:
🧣 Go and look at the pipes you can actually see. Loft, garage, under the floor, outside wall, cold cupboard.

Bare copper in an unheated space is the single most likely thing to burst in this country, and it's the cheapest thing in the world to prevent.

Where it matters most:

🥶 Loft pipework, especially anything above the insulation layer
🥶 Garage and outbuilding runs
🥶 The outside tap and the pipe feeding it
🥶 Anything in an unheated utility or porch

Foam lagging is a couple of pounds a length from any merchant. Slit it, push it on, tape the joints. Do the bends and the valve bodies too — that's where people stop and that's where pipes freeze.

And while you're there, learn where your stopcock is and check it actually turns. Finding out it's seized while water is coming through a ceiling is a bad way to learn.

Save this for when you need it.

posts.topic: Real job — the leak that was three metres from the damp patch
posts.facebook:
🔦 Real job: damp patch on a kitchen ceiling. Leak was three metres away.

This catches people out constantly, and it's why cutting a hole where the stain is usually achieves nothing but a hole.

Water doesn't drip straight down. It lands on a joist or the top of a plasterboard sheet and then travels — sometimes several metres — until it finds the lowest point or a gap to come through. The stain shows you where it exited, not where it started.

So the process is boring and it works. Isolate sections. Watch the pressure. Torch along the joist runs looking for the tide mark, because water leaves a trail even when it's dried.

In this case: a compression joint on a bathroom feed, weeping quietly, running the length of a joist before dropping through.

One fitting. Found without taking half a ceiling down.

posts.topic: Heating dies at 11pm — what to do

🌙 Boiler goes down late at night and the house starts cooling. Here's what to actually do.

1️⃣ Photograph the fault code and the pressure gauge. That's your diagnosis, sat right there.
2️⃣ Try one reset. One. If it locks out again immediately, stop — repeatedly resetting a boiler that's protecting itself can make things worse.
3️⃣ Close internal doors and shut curtains. A closed-up house holds heat surprisingly well overnight.
4️⃣ Run hot taps sparingly — if it's a combi you've got no stored hot water.
5️⃣ Smell gas? Don't touch switches. Get out, open doors, ring 0800 111 999.

Plain black Transit. Boring on purpose.

posts.facebook:
✅ It's never the big jobs. That's the thing nobody expects.

A full system install is a good week's work and a decent invoice, but the satisfaction is fairly flat. It's planned, it's methodical, you know how it ends before you start.

What actually stays with me:

🔎 A fault three other people couldn't find
🧹 A pipe run left tidier than I found it, even though nobody will ever see it
💬 Explaining something clearly enough that the customer explains it back to me correctly
🏠 Walking out of a house that's warm when it wasn't when I arrived
📞 A phone call two years later that starts with 'you probably don't remember me'

None of that shows up on an invoice. All of it is why I'm still doing this after all these years.

Whatever you do for work — what's the bit nobody sees that you're quietly proud of? Genuinely interested.
